 This word is used metaphorically also for strength ([Deut. 33:17](/deut#Deut.33.17)) and honour ([Job 16:15](/job#Job.16.15); [Lam. 2:3](/lam#Lam.2.3)). Horns are emblems of power, dominion, glory, and fierceness, as they are the chief means of attack and defence with the animals endowed with them ([Dan. 8:5](/dan#Dan.8.5), [9](/dan#Dan.8.9); [1 Sam. 2:1](/1sam#1Sam.2.1); [16:1](/1sam#1Sam.16.1), [13](/1sam#1Sam.16.13); [1 Kings 1:39](/1kgs#1Kgs.1.39); [22:11](/1kgs#1Kgs.22.11); [Josh. 6:4](/josh#Josh.6.4), [5](/josh#Josh.6.5); [Ps. 75:5](/ps#Ps.75.5), [10](/ps#Ps.75.10); 132:17; [Luke 1:69](/luke#Luke.1.69), etc.). The expression “horn of salvation,” applied to Christ, means a salvation of strength, or a strong Saviour ([Luke 1:69](/luke#Luke.1.69)). To have the horn “exalted” denotes prosperity and triumph ([Ps. 89:17](/ps#Ps.89.17), [24](/ps#Ps.89.24)). To “lift up” the horn is to act proudly ([Zech. 1:21](/zech#Zech.1.21)).

 Horns are also the symbol of royal dignity and power ([Jer. 48:25](/jer#Jer.48.25); [Zech. 1:18](/zech#Zech.1.18); [Dan. 8:24](/dan#Dan.8.24)).

recIepKRMvJyVHYvq.label: Hornet
recIepKRMvJyVHYvq.body: Heb. tsir’ah, “stinging”, ([Ex. 23:28](/exod#Exod.23.28); [Deut. 7:20](/deut#Deut.7.20); [Josh. 24:12](/josh#Josh.24.12)). The word is used in these passages as referring to some means by which the Canaanites were to be driven out from before the Israelites. Some have supposed that the word is used in a metaphorical sense as the symbol of some panic which would seize the people as a “terror of God” ([Gen. 35:5](/gen#Gen.35.5)), the consternation with which God would inspire the Canaanites. In Palestine there are four species of hornets, differing from our hornets, being larger in size, and they are very abundant. They “attack human beings in a very furious manner.” “The furious attack of a swarm of hornets drives cattle and horses to madness, and has even caused the death of the animals.”

recozQ9L2bE7tvzuO.label: Horonaim
recozQ9L2bE7tvzuO.body: Two caverns, a city of Moab to the south of the Arnon, built, apparently, upon an eminence, and a place of some importance ([Isa. 15:5](/isa#Isa.15.5); [Jer. 48:3](/jer#Jer.48.3), [5](/jer#Jer.48.5), [34](/jer#Jer.48.34)).

recpZlzKutNbnRgm7.label: Horonite
recpZlzKutNbnRgm7.body: The designation of Sanballat ([Neh. 2:10](/neh#Neh.2.10), [19](/neh#Neh.2.19)), a native of Horonaim, or of one of the two Beth-horons, the “upper” or the “nether,” mentioned in [Josh. 16:3](/josh#Josh.16.3), [5](/josh#Josh.16.5).

reck9aq3aOWCZlncd.label: Horse
reck9aq3aOWCZlncd.body: Always referred to in the Bible in connection with warlike operations, except [Isa. 28:28](/isa#Isa.28.28). The war-horse is described [Job 39:19-25](/job#Job.39.19). For a long period after their settlement in Canaan the Israelites made no use of horses, according to the prohibition, [Deut. 17:16](/deut#Deut.17.16). David was the first to form a force of cavalry ([2 Sam. 8:4](/2sam#2Sam.8.4)). But Solomon, from his connection with Egypt, greatly multiplied their number ([1 Kings 4:26](/1kgs#1Kgs.4.26); [10:26](/1kgs#1Kgs.10.26), [29](/1kgs#1Kgs.10.29)). After this, horses were freely used in Israel ([1 Kings 22:4](/1kgs#1Kgs.22.4); [2 Kings 3:7](/2kgs#2Kgs.3.7); [9:21](/2kgs#2Kgs.9.21), [33](/2kgs#2Kgs.9.33); [11:16](/2kgs#2Kgs.11.16)). The furniture of the horse consisted simply of a bridle ([Isa. 30:28](/isa#Isa.30.28)) and a curb ([Ps. 32:9](/ps#Ps.32.9)).

recbKXtpnUxnhebAy.label: Horse-gate
recbKXtpnUxnhebAy.body: A gate in the wall of Jerusalem, at the west end of the bridge, leading from Zion to the temple ([Neh. 3:28](/neh#Neh.3.28); [Jer. 31:40](/jer#Jer.31.40)).

recmPDZYXuPbtyvUh.label: Horse-leech
recmPDZYXuPbtyvUh.body: Occurs only in [Prov. 30:15](/prov#Prov.30.15) (Heb. ‘alukah); the generic name for any blood-sucking annelid. There are various species in the marshes and pools of Palestine. That here referred to, the Hoemopis, is remarkable for the coarseness of its bite, and is therefore not used for medical purposes. They are spoken of in the East with feelings of aversion and horror, because of their propensity to fasten on the tongue and nostrils of horses when they come to drink out of the pools. The medicinal leech (Hirudo medicinalis), besides other species of leeches, are common in the waters of Syria.

recJKaoGucdjvPN5Y.label: Horseman
recJKaoGucdjvPN5Y.body: Heb. ba’al parash, “master of a horse.” The “horsemen” mentioned [Ex. 14:9](/exod#Exod.14.9) were “mounted men”, i.e., men who rode in chariots. The army of Pharaoh consisted of a chariot and infantry force. We find that at a later period, however, the Egyptians had cavalry ([2 Chr. 12:3](/2chr#2Chr.12.3)).

rec1IOtvfNPJHL7Po.label: Hosah
rec1IOtvfNPJHL7Po.body: A place on the border of the tribe of Asher ([Josh. 19:29](/josh#Josh.19.29)), a little to the south of Zidon.

recir6WFRccRRntdD.label: Hosah
recir6WFRccRRntdD.body: A Levite of the family of Merari ([1 Chr. 16:38](/1chr#1Chr.16.38)).

recMKg6n5Irek5UD8.label: Hosanna
recMKg6n5Irek5UD8.body: Save now! or Save, we beseech, ([Matt. 21:9](/matt#Matt.21.9)). This was a customary form of acclamation at the feast of Tabernacles. (Comp. [Ps. 118:25](/ps#Ps.118.25).)

recqj4w6hWmBiGC8o.label: Hosea
recqj4w6hWmBiGC8o.body: Salvation, the son of Beeri, and author of the book of prophecies bearing his name. He belonged to the kingdom of Israel. “His Israelitish origin is attested by the peculiar, rough, Aramaizing diction, pointing to the northern part of Palestine; by the intimate acquaintance he evinces with the localities of Ephraim (5:1; 6:8, 9; 12:12; 14:6, etc.); by passages like 1:2, where the kingdom is styled ‘the land’, and 7:5, where the Israelitish king is designated as ‘our’ king.” The period of his ministry (extending to some sixty years) is indicated in the superscription ([Hos. 1:1](/hos#Hos.1.1), [2](/hos#Hos.1.2)). He is the only prophet of Israel who has left any written prophecy.

recxAgN0ZSuoJKzxo.label: Hosea, Prophecies of
recxAgN0ZSuoJKzxo.body:
This book stands first in order among the “Minor Prophets.” “The probable cause of the location of Hosea may be the thoroughly national character of his oracles, their length, their earnest tone, and vivid representations.” This was the longest of the prophetic books written before the Captivity. Hosea prophesied in a dark and melancholy period of Israel’s history, the period of Israel’s decline and fall. Their sins had brought upon them great national disasters. “Their homicides and fornication, their perjury and theft, their idolatry and impiety, are censured and satirized with a faithful severity.” He was a contemporary of Isaiah. The book may be divided into two parts, the first containing chapters 1-3, and symbolically representing the idolatry of Israel under imagery borrowed from the matrimonial relation. The figures of marriage and adultery are common in the Old Testament writings to represent the spiritual relations between Jehovah and the people of Israel. Here we see the apostasy of Israel and their punishment, with their future repentance, forgiveness, and restoration.

 The second part, containing 4-14, is a summary of Hosea’s discourses, filled with denunciations, threatenings, exhortations, promises, and revelations of mercy.

 Quotations from Hosea are found in [Matt. 2:15](/matt#Matt.2.15); [9:15](/matt#Matt.9.15); [12:7](/matt#Matt.12.7); [Rom. 9:25](/rom#Rom.9.25), [26](/rom#Rom.9.26). There are, in addition, various allusions to it in other places ([Luke 23:30](/luke#Luke.23.30); [Rev. 6:16](/rev#Rev.6.16), comp. [Hos. 10:8](/hos#Hos.10.8); [Rom. 9:25](/rom#Rom.9.25), [26](/rom#Rom.9.26); [1 Pet. 2:10](/1pet#1Pet.2.10), comp. [Hos. 1:10](/hos#Hos.1.10), etc.).

 As regards the style of this writer, it has been said that “each verse forms a whole for itself, like one heavy toll in a funeral knell.” “Inversions (7:8; 9:11, 13; 12: 8), anacolutha (9:6; 12:8, etc.), ellipses (9:4; 13:9, etc.), paranomasias, and plays upon words, are very characteristic of Hosea (8:7; 9:15; 10:5; 11:5; 12:11).”

recYUtyBLM7FouKEP.label: Hoshea
recYUtyBLM7FouKEP.body: The original name of the son of Nun, afterwards called Joshua ([Num. 13:8](/num#Num.13.8), [16](/num#Num.13.16); [Deut. 32:44](/deut#Deut.32.44)).

recIOspMCSJVra3v4.label: Hoshea
recIOspMCSJVra3v4.body: [1 Chr. 27:20](/1chr#1Chr.27.20). The ruler of Ephraim in David’s time.

rec2MkkV3q7vr7UjK.label: Hoshea
rec2MkkV3q7vr7UjK.body: The last king of Israel. He conspired against and slew his predecessor, Pekah ([Isa. 7:16](/isa#Isa.7.16)), but did not ascend the throne till after an interregnum of warfare of eight years ([2 Kings 17:1](/2kgs#2Kgs.17.1), [2](/2kgs#2Kgs.17.2)). Soon after this he submitted to Shalmaneser, the Assyrian king, who a second time invaded the land to punish Hoshea, because of his withholding tribute which he had promised to pay. A second revolt brought back the Assyrian king Sargon, who besieged Samaria, and carried the ten tribes away beyond the Euphrates, B.C. 720 ([2 Kings 17:5](/2kgs#2Kgs.17.5), [6](/2kgs#2Kgs.17.6); 18:9-12). No more is heard of Hoshea. He disappeared like “foam upon the water” ([Hos. 10:7](/hos#Hos.10.7); [13:11](/hos#Hos.13.11)).

receQuyMKBjMCDYf4.label: Host
receQuyMKBjMCDYf4.body:
An entertainer ([Rom. 16:23](/rom#Rom.16.23)); a tavern-keeper, the keeper of a caravansary ([Luke 10:35](/luke#Luke.10.35)).

 In warfare, a troop or military force. This consisted at first only of infantry. Solomon afterwards added cavalry ([1 Kings 4:26](/1kgs#1Kgs.4.26); [10:26](/1kgs#1Kgs.10.26)). Every male Israelite from twenty to fifty years of age was bound by the law to bear arms when necessary ([Num. 1:3](/num#Num.1.3); [26:2](/num#Num.26.2); [2 Chr. 25:5](/2chr#2Chr.25.5)).

 Saul was the first to form a standing army ([1 Sam. 13:2](/1sam#1Sam.13.2); [24:2](/1sam#1Sam.24.2)). This example was followed by David ([1 Chr. 27:1](/1chr#1Chr.27.1)), and Solomon ([1 Kings 4:26](/1kgs#1Kgs.4.26)), and by the kings of Israel and Judah ([2 Chr. 17:14](/2chr#2Chr.17.14); [26:11](/2chr#2Chr.26.11); [2 Kings 11:4](/2kgs#2Kgs.11.4), etc.).

recpWt0ggAV23i4zI.label: Host of heaven
recpWt0ggAV23i4zI.body: The sun, moon, and stars are so designated ([Gen. 2:1](/gen#Gen.2.1)). When the Jews fell into idolatry they worshipped these ([Deut. 4:19](/deut#Deut.4.19); [2 Kings 17:16](/2kgs#2Kgs.17.16); [21:3](/2kgs#2Kgs.21.3), [5](/2kgs#2Kgs.21.5); [23:5](/2kgs#2Kgs.23.5); [Jer. 19:13](/jer#Jer.19.13); [Zeph. 1:5](/zeph#Zeph.1.5); [Acts 7:42](/acts#Acts.7.42)).

rectKH2MeWb2KNAFn.label: Hostage
rectKH2MeWb2KNAFn.body: A person delivered into the hands of another as a security for the performance of some promise, etc. ([2 Kings 14:14](/2kgs#2Kgs.14.14); [2 Chr. 25:24](/2chr#2Chr.25.24)).

recVXpdmuV8SM6q9c.label: Hough
recVXpdmuV8SM6q9c.body: To hamstring, i.e., sever the “tendon of Achilles” of the hinder legs of captured horses ([Josh. 11:6](/josh#Josh.11.6); [2 Sam. 8:4](/2sam#2Sam.8.4); [1 Chr. 18:4](/1chr#1Chr.18.4)), so as to render them useless.

recaA6cMD3hBuX0TV.label: Hour
recaA6cMD3hBuX0TV.body:
First found in [Dan. 3:6](/dan#Dan.3.6); [4:19](/dan#Dan.4.19), [33](/dan#Dan.4.33);[5:5](/dan#Dan.5.5). It is the rendering of the Chaldee shaah, meaning a “moment,” a “look.” It is used in the New Testament frequently to denote some determinate season ([Matt. 8:13](/matt#Matt.8.13); [Luke 12:39](/luke#Luke.12.39)).

 With the ancient Hebrews the divisions of the day were “morning, evening, and noon-day” ([Ps. 55:17](/ps#Ps.55.17), etc.). The Greeks, following the Babylonians, divided the day into twelve hours. The Jews, during the Captivity, learned also from the Babylonians this method of dividing time. When Judea became subject to the Romans, the Jews adopted the Roman mode of reckoning time. The night was divided into four watches ([Luke 12:38](/luke#Luke.12.38); [Matt. 14:25](/matt#Matt.14.25); [13:25](/matt#Matt.13.25)). Frequent allusion is also made to hours ([Matt. 25:13](/matt#Matt.25.13); [26:40](/matt#Matt.26.40), etc.).

 An hour was the twelfth part of the day, reckoning from sunrise to sunset, and consequently it perpetually varied in length.

recV5ycjE51qExr0t.label: House
recV5ycjE51qExr0t.body:
Till their sojourn in Egypt the Hebrews dwelt in tents. They then for the first time inhabited cities ([Gen. 47:3](/gen#Gen.47.3); [Ex. 12:7](/exod#Exod.12.7); [Heb. 11:9](/heb#Heb.11.9)). From the earliest times the Assyrians and the Canaanites were builders of cities. The Hebrews after the Conquest took possession of the captured cities, and seem to have followed the methods of building that had been pursued by the Canaanites. Reference is made to the stone ([1 Kings 7:9](/1kgs#1Kgs.7.9); [Isa. 9:10](/isa#Isa.9.10)) and marble ([1 Chr. 29:2](/1chr#1Chr.29.2)) used in building, and to the internal wood-work of the houses ([1 Kings 6:15](/1kgs#1Kgs.6.15); [7:2](/1kgs#1Kgs.7.2); [10:11](/1kgs#1Kgs.10.11), [12](/1kgs#1Kgs.10.12); [2 Chr. 3:5](/2chr#2Chr.3.5); [Jer. 22:14](/jer#Jer.22.14)). “Ceiled houses” were such as had beams inlaid in the walls to which wainscotting was fastened ([Ezra 6:4](/ezra#Ezra.6.4); [Jer. 22:14](/jer#Jer.22.14); [Hag. 1:4](/hag#Hag.1.4)). “Ivory houses” had the upper parts of the walls adorned with figures in stucco with gold and ivory ([1 Kings 22:39](/1kgs#1Kgs.22.39); [2 Chr. 3:6](/2chr#2Chr.3.6); [Ps. 45:8](/ps#Ps.45.8)).

 The roofs of the dwelling-houses were flat, and are often alluded to in Scripture ([2 Sam. 11:2](/2sam#2Sam.11.2); [Isa. 22:1](/isa#Isa.22.1); [Matt. 24:17](/matt#Matt.24.17)). Sometimes tents or booths were erected on them ([2 Sam. 16:22](/2sam#2Sam.16.22)). They were protected by parapets or low walls ([Deut. 22:8](/deut#Deut.22.8)). On the house-tops grass sometimes grew ([Prov. 19:13](/prov#Prov.19.13); [27:15](/prov#Prov.27.15); [Ps. 129:6](/ps#Ps.129.6), [7](/ps#Ps.129.7)). They were used, not only as places of recreation in the evening, but also sometimes as sleeping-places at night ([1 Sam. 9:25](/1sam#1Sam.9.25), [26](/1sam#1Sam.9.26); [2 Sam. 11:2](/2sam#2Sam.11.2); [16:22](/2sam#2Sam.16.22); [Dan. 4:29](/dan#Dan.4.29); [Job 27:18](/job#Job.27.18); [Prov. 21:9](/prov#Prov.21.9)), and as places of devotion ([Jer. 32:29](/jer#Jer.32.29); [19:13](/jer#Jer.19.13)).

rec9ywBwS6Zfu5BXr.label: Hukkok
rec9ywBwS6Zfu5BXr.body: Decreed, a town near Zebulun, not far from Jordan, on the border of Naphtali ([Josh. 19:34](/josh#Josh.19.34)).

recvnBQ6jVWjSWfML.label: Hul
recvnBQ6jVWjSWfML.body: Circle, the second son of Aram ([Gen. 10:23](/gen#Gen.10.23)), and grandson of Shem.

receTAuN4DMKxeJOn.label: Huldah
receTAuN4DMKxeJOn.body: Weasel, a prophetess; the wife of Shallum. She was consulted regarding the “book of the law” discovered by the high priest Hilkiah ([2 Kings 22:14-20](/2kgs#2Kgs.22.14); [2 Chr. 34:22-28](/2chr#2Chr.34.22)). She resided in that part of Jerusalem called the Mishneh (A.V., “the college;” R.V., “the second quarter”), supposed by some to be the suburb between the inner and the outer wall, the second or lower city, Akra. Miriam ([Ex. 15:20](/exod#Exod.15.20)) and Deborah ([Judg. 4:4](/judg#Judg.4.4)) are the only others who bear the title of “prophetess,” for the word in [Isa. 8:3](/isa#Isa.8.3) means only the prophet’s wife.

recxEzEqwPBsx3Rl7.label: Humiliation of Christ
recxEzEqwPBsx3Rl7.body:
([Phil. 2:8](/phil#Phil.2.8)), seen in (1) his birth ([Gal. 4:4](/gal#Gal.4.4); [Luke 2:7](/luke#Luke.2.7); [John 1:46](/john#John.1.46); [Heb. 2:9](/heb#Heb.2.9)), (2) his circumstances, (3) his reputation ([Isa. 53](/isa#Isa.53); [Matt. 26:59](/matt#Matt.26.59), [67](/matt#Matt.26.67); [Ps. 22:6](/ps#Ps.22.6); [Matt. 26:68](/matt#Matt.26.68)), (4) his soul ([Ps. 22:1](/ps#Ps.22.1); [Matt. 4:1-11](/matt#Matt.4.1); [Luke 22:44](/luke#Luke.22.44); [Heb. 2:17](/heb#Heb.2.17), [18](/heb#Heb.2.18); 4:15), (5) his death ([Luke 23](/luke#Luke.23); [John 19](/john#John.19); [Mark 15:24](/mark#Mark.15.24), [25](/mark#Mark.15.25)), (6) and his burial ([Isa. 53:9](/isa#Isa.53.9); [Matt. 27:57](/matt#Matt.27.57), [58](/matt#Matt.27.58), [60](/matt#Matt.27.60)).

 His humiliation was necessary (1) to execute the purpose of God ([Acts 2:23](/acts#Acts.2.23), [24](/acts#Acts.2.24); [Ps. 40:6-8](/ps#Ps.40.6)), (2) fulfil the Old Testament types and prophecies, (3) satisfy the law in the room of the guilty ([Isa. 53](/isa#Isa.53); [Heb. 9:12](/heb#Heb.9.12), [15](/heb#Heb.9.15)), procure for them eternal redemption, (4) and to show us an example.

rec4JvNVD9V4otygN.label: Humility
rec4JvNVD9V4otygN.body:
A prominent Christian grace ([Rom. 12:3](/rom#Rom.12.3); [15:17](/rom#Rom.15.17), [18](/rom#Rom.15.18); [1 Cor. 3:5-7](/1cor#1Cor.3.5); [2 Cor. 3:5](/2cor#2Cor.3.5); [Phil. 4:11-13](/phil#Phil.4.11)). It is a state of mind well pleasing to God ([1 Pet. 3:4](/1pet#1Pet.3.4)); it preserves the soul in tranquillity ([Ps. 69:32](/ps#Ps.69.32), [33](/ps#Ps.69.33)), and makes us patient under trials ([Job 1:22](/job#Job.1.22)).

 Christ has set us an example of humility ([Phil. 2:6-8](/phil#Phil.2.6)). We should be led thereto by a remembrance of our sins ([Lam. 3:39](/lam#Lam.3.39)), and by the thought that it is the way to honour ([Prov. 16:18](/prov#Prov.16.18)), and that the greatest promises are made to the humble ([Ps. 147:6](/ps#Ps.147.6); [Isa. 57:15](/isa#Isa.57.15); [66:2](/isa#Isa.66.2); [1 Pet. 5:5](/1pet#1Pet.5.5)). It is a “great paradox in Christianity that it makes humility the avenue to glory.”

recE4eAppJDRo1GKE.label: Hunting
recE4eAppJDRo1GKE.body:
Mentioned first in [Gen. 10:9](/gen#Gen.10.9) in connection with Nimrod. Esau was “a cunning hunter” ([Gen. 25:27](/gen#Gen.25.27)). Hunting was practised by the Hebrews after their settlement in the “Land of Promise” ([Lev. 17:15](/lev#Lev.17.15); [Prov. 12:27](/prov#Prov.12.27)). The lion and other ravenous beasts were found in Palestine ([1 Sam. 17:34](/1sam#1Sam.17.34); [2 Sam. 23:20](/2sam#2Sam.23.20); [1 Kings 13:24](/1kgs#1Kgs.13.24); [Ezek. 19:3-8](/ezek#Ezek.19.3)), and it must have been necessary to hunt and destroy them. Various snares and gins were used in hunting ([Ps. 91:3](/ps#Ps.91.3); [Amos 3:5](/amos#Amos.3.5); [2 Sam. 23:20](/2sam#2Sam.23.20)).

 War is referred to under the idea of hunting ([Jer. 16:16](/jer#Jer.16.16); [Ezek. 32:30](/ezek#Ezek.32.30)).

recGURX8wUsdiECdx.label: Hur
recGURX8wUsdiECdx.body: A hole, as of a viper, etc.

recJVvihnBHnmKBIa.label: Hur
recJVvihnBHnmKBIa.body: The husband of Miriam, Moses’ sister ([Ex. 17:10-12](/exod#Exod.17.10)). He was associated with Aaron in charge of the people when Moses was absent on Sinai ([Ex. 24:14](/exod#Exod.24.14)). He was probably of the tribe of Judah, and grandfather of Bezaleel ([Ex. 31:2](/exod#Exod.31.2); [35:30](/exod#Exod.35.30); [1 Chr. 2:19](/1chr#1Chr.2.19)).

receVk6sBYr1FQK6Z.label: Hur
receVk6sBYr1FQK6Z.body: One of the five princes of Midian who were defeated and slain by the Israelites under the command of Phinehas ([Num. 31:8](/num#Num.31.8)).

recQ3XT9jLtdtLd0P.label: Hurai
recQ3XT9jLtdtLd0P.body: Linen-worker, one of David’s heroes, a native of the valley of Mount Gaash ([1 Chr. 11:32](/1chr#1Chr.11.32)).

recv4advywQlWsM1Y.label: Husband
recv4advywQlWsM1Y.body: I.e., the “house-band,” connecting and keeping together the whole family. A man when betrothed was esteemed from that time a husband ([Matt. 1:16](/matt#Matt.1.16), [20](/matt#Matt.1.20); [Luke 2:5](/luke#Luke.2.5)). A recently married man was exempt from going to war for “one year” ([Deut. 20:7](/deut#Deut.20.7); [24:5](/deut#Deut.24.5)).

recwAGFsa932KiNPM.label: Husbandman
recwAGFsa932KiNPM.body: One whose business it is to cultivate the ground. It was one of the first occupations, and was esteemed most honourable ([Gen. 9:20](/gen#Gen.9.20); [26:12](/gen#Gen.26.12), [14](/gen#Gen.26.14); [37:7](/gen#Gen.37.7), etc.). All the Hebrews, except those engaged in religious services, were husbandmen.

recrovbO0C6RPDqSt.label: Hushai
recrovbO0C6RPDqSt.body: Quick, “the Archite,” “the king’s friend” ([1 Chr. 27:33](/1chr#1Chr.27.33)). When David fled from Jerusalem, on account of the rebellion of Absalom, and had reached the summit of Olivet, he there met Hushai, whom he sent back to Jerusalem for the purpose of counteracting the influence of Ahithophel, who had joined the ranks of Absalom ([2 Sam. 15:32](/2sam#2Sam.15.32), [37](/2sam#2Sam.15.37); 16:16-18). It was by his advice that Absalom refrained from immediately pursuing after David. By this delay the cause of Absalom was ruined, for it gave David time to muster his forces.

recXocGN6gKBhatFK.label: Husk
recXocGN6gKBhatFK.body: In [Num. 6:4](/num#Num.6.4) (Heb. zag) it means the “skin” of a grape. In [2 Kings 4:42](/2kgs#2Kgs.4.42) (Heb. tsiqlon) it means a “sack” for grain, as rendered in the Revised Version. In [Luke 15:16](/luke#Luke.15.16), in the parable of the Prodigal Son, it designates the beans of the carob tree, or Ceratonia siliqua. From the supposition, mistaken, however, that it was on the husks of this tree that John the Baptist fed, it is called “St. John’s bread” and “locust tree.” This tree is in “February covered with innumerable purple-red pendent blossoms, which ripen in April and May into large crops of pods from 6 to 10 inches long, flat, brown, narrow, and bent like a horn (whence the Greek name keratia, meaning ‘little horns’), with a sweetish taste when still unripe. Enormous quantities of these are gathered for sale in various towns and for exportation.” “They were eaten as food, though only by the poorest of the poor, in the time of our Lord.” The bean is called a “gerah,” which is used as the name of the smallest Hebrew weight, twenty of these making a shekel.

recvyqHV0o4VGVmoU.label: Hymn
recvyqHV0o4VGVmoU.body:
Occurs only [Eph. 5:19](/eph#Eph.5.19) and [Col. 3:16](/col#Col.3.16). The verb to “sing an hymn” occurs [Matt. 26:30](/matt#Matt.26.30) and [Mark 14:26](/mark#Mark.14.26). The same Greek word is rendered to “sing praises” [Acts 16:25](/acts#Acts.16.25) (R.V., “sing hymns”) and [Heb. 2:12](/heb#Heb.2.12). The “hymn” which our Lord sang with his disciples at the last Supper is generally supposed to have been the latter part of the Hallel, comprehending [Ps. 113](/ps#Ps.113)-118. It was thus a name given to a number of psalms taken together and forming a devotional exercise.

 The noun hymn is used only with reference to the services of the Greeks, and was distinguished from the psalm. The Greek tunes required Greek hymns. Our information regarding the hymnology of the early Christians is very limited.

rechLvRqqhYsF4fY0.label: Hypocrite
rechLvRqqhYsF4fY0.body: One who puts on a mask and feigns himself to be what he is not; a dissembler in religion. Our Lord severely rebuked the scribes and Pharisees for their hypocrisy ([Matt. 6:2](/matt#Matt.6.2), [5](/matt#Matt.6.5), [16](/matt#Matt.6.16)). “The hypocrite’s hope shall perish” ([Job 8:13](/job#Job.8.13)). The Hebrew word here rendered “hypocrite” rather means the “godless” or “profane,” as it is rendered in [Jer. 23:11](/jer#Jer.23.11), i.e., polluted with crimes.

recTlG52DeJTV7fwZ.label: Hyssop
recTlG52DeJTV7fwZ.body: (Heb. ‘ezob; LXX. hyssopos), first mentioned in [Ex. 12:22](/exod#Exod.12.22) in connection with the institution of the Passover. We find it afterwards mentioned in [Lev. 14:4](/lev#Lev.14.4), [6](/lev#Lev.14.6), [52](/lev#Lev.14.52); [Num. 19:6](/num#Num.19.6), [18](/num#Num.19.18); [Heb. 9:19](/heb#Heb.9.19). It is spoken of as a plant “springing out of the wall” ([1 Kings 4:33](/1kgs#1Kgs.4.33)). Many conjectures have been formed as to what this plant really was. Some contend that it was a species of marjoram (origanum), six species of which are found in Palestine. Others with more probability think that it was the caper plant, the Capparis spinosa of Linnaeus. This plant grew in Egypt, in the desert of Sinai, and in Palestine. It was capable of producing a stem three or four feet in length ([Matt. 27:48](/matt#Matt.27.48); [Mark 15:36](/mark#Mark.15.36). Comp. [John 19:29](/john#John.19.29)).
